title: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’
description: Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue. You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without
body: Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue. You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without a check-in or an impulse purchase that should have been discussed. Then suddenly you've stopped talking about that thing and started talking about each other: "Why are you overreacting?""You always do this.""You're being impossible right now."One minute you're trying to solve a problem together, and the next you're each trying to prove you're the more reasonable person in the room. And once an argument becomes about that, it can't really be resolved. Because now, the battlefield and ammunition are endless.As a psychologist who studies couples, I know that, thankfully, there's a practice that can act as a guardrail for disagreements. I call it a partial yield, and it prevents this all-too-familiar detour.What a 'partial yield' sounds likeA partial yield is a type of phrase you use when you concede the specific piece of the argument you're genuinely responsible for, the moment it comes up, without conceding the rest of your position. It usually sounds very ordinary:"You're right, that part's on me." "That's fair, I did forget to tell you." "I shouldn't have made that decision without talking to you first." So you're not agreeing that you were wrong about everything. But you are admitting the fault that's actually yours, before your partner has to pry it out of you.In my experience, nothing de-escalates a conflict faster.Why a 'partial yield' works so quicklyWhen your partner confronts you, some part of them is preemptively braced for the effort of convincing you. It's why voices get louder and why examples start piling up. They're not trying to hurt you. They're trying to get you to believe them, and they've assumed it's going to be hard.A partial yield releases the pent-up steam that can otherwise fuel an escalation. The effect is palpable almost immediately, and it rarely feels like a defeat for either person. Your partner gets the acknowledgment they were pushing for, and you get to be honest about your part without signing away the rest.It's also easier on you than a full apology, which matters more than you might think. Most of us don't withhold small admissions because we believe we did nothing wrong. We withhold them because admitting to one thing feels like admitting to all the rest, too, and we'd rather concede nothing than concede everything. What happens when you skip this stepI'd pay attention to what happens when you don't use a partial yield phrase.If you never take accountability in the moment, the problem doesn't just go away. Your partner notices and files it away. They might bring it up again three weeks from now in the middle of an unrelated argument. It may look like score-keeping, but more often it's an old grievance that never got heard and owned, finally finding an opening.Couples who concede small things routinely don't build up much of that "back-pocket" inventory, so there's nothing to reach for at a moment's notice. Their arguments tend to stay roughly within the context of whatever caused them.How to use the 'partial yield' effectivelyA few steps differentiate a real partial yield from a fake one:Be specific about what you're claiming. "You're right, I shouldn't have said it like that in front of your mom," works. A vague "Okay, fine, I was wrong!" reads as surrender under protest, and your partner will hear it that way.Don't attach a "but." "You're right, that part's on me, but you also…" cancels the whole thing. If you have a counterpoint, it will survive the next 90 seconds. Let the concession stand alone first.Do it early. The yield loses most of its power once someone has already started listing their old grievances. The ideal moment is the first time you notice you're technically in the wrong about something small, which is usually much earlier than we like to admit.Say it even when you're mostly right. Especially then. Being mostly right is the most common reason people refuse to concede anything at all.In my experience, genuine partial yields are the difference between couples who argue about — and solve — problems and couples who get stuck arguing about each other.Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org.

schema.headline: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’

title: I work hard to stay close to my friends. A researcher says it’s good for my well-being—and these 3 habits can help
description: Not to brag, but without realizing it, I've become a model friend — someone my loved ones admire for how well I maintain my relationships. At least, s
body: Not to brag, but without realizing it, I've become a model friend — someone my loved ones admire for how well I maintain my relationships. At least, so they tell me.Last month, my closest friend asked me for pointers on how to stay connected to her community while balancing work, well-being and everything else in her life. It's no easy feat. Loneliness levels in the U.S. are high, and instead of turning to each other, many people reach for their tech devices, found an American Psychiatric Association poll published on May 12. Eight percent of Americans report having zero close friends, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey of about 5,000 U.S. adults.Some businesses now offer to facilitate the friendship process, offering summer camps for adults or guidance from friendship coaches that can sometimes cost thousands of dollars. And when you do form friendships, you could grow apart for a number of reasons, says Jessica D. Ayers, an assistant professor of psychological science at Boise State University: classic ones like moving to a different state for a new job or being in different stages of life, or newer ones like trying to keep up with each other on social media and forgetting to keep in touch outside of your smartphones.Especially if your friends have busy lives or don't often reach out to make plans, putting in the work to stay in touch may seem like a fundamentally selfless gesture. In fact, making the effort to maintain friendships can benefit you too, says Ayers, who researches the science of friendship and how to maintain connections. Staying in touch with friends can improve well-being, lower levels of depression and loneliness, decrease anxiety, and even "increase our chances of survival after things like major surgery," she says.The benefit is mutual for both parties, Ayers says, especially in "long-lasting and sustained relationships." And a high degree of social fitness contributes to a longer, healthier and more fulfilled life, according to an ongoing 88-year-old Harvard University happiness study. Put simply, your friendships can help you succeed.Staying in touch can require a lot of hard work, at least on paper. I didn't fully realize this until I considered just how many strategies I have for keeping in contact with my community. I set up multiple one-on-one hangouts per month with a rotating cast of friends, clear time in my calendar to be present for my loved ones' birthday celebrations and stay up-to-date in five-plus group chats with friends and family.In a sense, I was trained to do this: I have five siblings, and growing up in our household, showing up for each other was a non-negotiable. But there's more to it. Whenever a friend crosses my mind, I reach out to them, just to see how they're doing or ask when we can hang out in the near future. I host small get-togethers — one of my favorites was an October 2025 party themed around the movie "Coraline." I travel to visit my friends who live in different states at least once a year, or plan vacations together with them.Ayers says she approves of my practices. Even the simple act of sending a friend a quick note because you briefly thought about them is "a brilliant practice," she says, adding: "It is the best thing you can do."The first step: 'Just reach out' to your friendsTo keep your friendships healthy and strong, Ayers recommends three things:"Just reach out to them," she says. It doesn't have to be super frequent, but let your friends know you value them: "When they come to your mind, send them a text, 'Hey, thinking of you.'" Prioritize relationships built on intrinsic qualities over external ones, Ayers recommends. Friendships based on shared values like loyalty and honesty are often much more meaningful than connections built on more superficial qualities, she says.Bring something to the table in each friendship, and expend a reasonable amount of time, resources and energy to show up for your friends — even if, sometimes, you'd rather stay home. In other words, be the friend you'd want others to be to you. "Remembering that you are a valued person in this relationship is important," says Ayers.Ayers and her best friend live in different states — Idaho and California, respectively — she says. They send each other voice memos throughout the week, ranging from quick check-ins to 15-minute breakdowns of an important update, she says.But especially with friends who live nearby, you should take your conversations offline whenever you can, Ayers says. Even in group chats, she says, you can write something like: "'Hey, I'm going to come see you in person ... We [should] go to this coffee shop and just hang out,' instead of relying solely on the technology aspect to mediate."You can even invite your friends into your regular schedule, without having to find extra time in your calendar. Ask a friend to tag along when you're running errands, or doing some other low-pressure activity, suggests Ayers. She invites her friends to her children's sporting events, she says: "We can catch up in between our kids going to bat, or our kids' time on the soccer field, and it's a lot less pressure because there's no expectations there."Being a social person has trade-offs. I'm not sure I've had a free weekend all year. But knowing I've built a community that I can rely on, and vice versa, brings me a worthwhile peace of mind. I'll sacrifice a day of couch-rotting to watch my favorite show for a night of off-key karaoke or baking brownies at midnight with my homegirls in a heartbeat, time and time again.
